title: Anger (Matthew 5:21–26)
hook: before you bring your gift, go and be reconciled

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Torah, and Jesus saying he came not to destroy but to fulfill. Did you ask what something old was for? Day two hundred forty-three.

Thou shalt not kill. It sounds like a commandment almost anyone could keep. But then there's the name muttered under the breath at a brother or sister. The furious speech rehearsed in the shower, to someone who isn't there. Walking into church, or a family dinner, or a meeting, while someone in the room is still upset, and just carrying on. Yesterday Jesus said: go deeper, to the heart. Today he shows what that means, starting with one of the Ten Commandments.
screen: `THOU SHALT NOT KILL.` → `A FURIOUS SPEECH IN THE SHOWER.` → `DEEPER, TO THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Ye have heard, he says, that it was said, thou shalt not kill. But I say unto you: whoever is angry with his brother is in danger of judgment. And whoever calls him raca, an insult usually explained as Aramaic for empty-head, is in danger too. This is the first of several times in this chapter Jesus says ye have heard, but I say unto you. He isn't canceling the commandment. He's following it back to its root. Murder starts somewhere: in contempt, in the name you call someone, in the grudge you feed. Then Jesus tells a small, practical story. In the King James Bible: "Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift." Picture it. You've traveled to the temple with a gift to offer. You're at the altar. And you remember that someone has something against you. Not that you're angry with them. That they're angry with you. Jesus says: leave the gift right there. Go. Make it right. Then come back. The Greek word is diallasso: to be reconciled, to make things up with someone. In other words, the relationship with your neighbor isn't separate from your worship. Christians say God cares about both, and here the neighbor comes first.
screen: `YE HAVE HEARD, BUT I SAY.` · `RACA: EMPTY-HEAD.` · `LEAVE THY GIFT BEFORE THE ALTAR.` · `THEY HAVE SOMETHING AGAINST YOU.` · then, large: `FIRST BE RECONCILED TO THY BROTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reach out to someone you're angry with, or someone who's angry with you. Settle, and breathe. Remember the twist in the story: it's the other person who has something against you. Let one such face come to mind. Notice any anger, yours or theirs, without feeding it. You don't have to fix everything today. Just picture what leaving the gift and going might look like: a knock on a door, a call, I'm sorry for my part. If it isn't safe to reach out, simply let the anger rest for these two minutes. If you pray, you can bring that person with you into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Anger. Jesus follows thou shalt not kill back to its root, and says: before your gift, go and be reconciled.
Your line: reconcile first. Today, before one important thing you do, take one first step toward someone who has something against you. Day two hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: In churches that share the peace during the service, it often comes before the gifts are brought to the altar or before communion, a custom some link to this passage, and some Christians make a point of mending quarrels before receiving communion or before Easter.

trapdoor: what you thought: as long as you don't hurt anyone, anger is fine.
what it means: Jesus traces murder back to contempt, and puts making peace ahead of worship.
what a scholar hears: raca is usually explained as Aramaic for empty-head, and the pattern ye have heard, but I say begins here.

notes: raca: generally explained as Aramaic reqa, 'empty (-headed)'; confirm.
eike ('without a cause') in Matthew 5:22 is absent from P64/P67, Sinaiticus (first hand) and Vaticanus; confirm 'the oldest manuscripts don't have those words'.
Six antitheses in Matthew 5 (21, 27, 31, 33, 38, 43): confirm the count.
diallasso 'to be changed toward': etymological gloss (dia + allasso, to change); confirm.
The practice adds a safety line for cases where reaching out isn't safe.
